**A backdoor can be narrow enough to evade ordinary validation.** The model may behave normally on common inputs but fail under a particular condition. Therefore high average accuracy after training or mitigation does not establish that all conditional behavior is clean. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)

The number “500 poisoned examples” alone says little about success. Dataset size, duplication, influence, model capacity, and training procedure all matter. Controlled research demonstrates possible persistence; it does not prove that every unusual response is evidence of deliberate poisoning.

**Defensive work starts with provenance and controlled evaluation.** Restrict dataset changes, record source and version lineage, and investigate unexpected clusters or label changes. Use trusted held-out data and targeted evaluation slices in an isolated environment.

After mitigation, retest both ordinary utility and the suspected conditional failure, and retain rollback options. A generic safety-tuning pass is not proof of removal. Conversely, avoid accusing a source based on one anomalous output: distinguish reproducible conditional behavior, accidental model error, and evidence of malicious data modification.

**Technical details and references.**

Five hundred poisoned examples can be consequential, but the count alone predicts neither success nor detectability: dataset size, duplication, model capacity, trigger coverage, and training choices matter. A backdoor can preserve ordinary validation accuracy while changing behavior on a narrow condition. Controlled sleeper-agent research illustrates why subsequent safety training is not proof that a backdoor was removed. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05566)

Defensively preserve data provenance, audit unexpected clusters and label changes, constrain dataset access, and compare clean and targeted evaluation slices in an isolated environment. Use trusted held-out data, model/version lineage, and rollback. Test for persistence after mitigation and monitor suspicious conditional behavior. Do not infer cleanliness from average benchmark scores; equally, an unusual input response is not sufficient evidence that deliberate poisoning occurred.
